title: Generics, variance, exceptions, interfaces and modern types
scopeHtml: Scope: generics and erasure, variance (PECS), exception design, interfaces vs abstract classes, default methods, sealed types, records and data classes.

notes.title: Generics basics and type erasure
notes.html:
Generics let one class or method work with many types while the compiler checks safety. List<String> cannot accept an Integer; the error appears at compile time, not as a ClassCastException in production.

Java implements generics by type erasure: the compiler checks types, then removes them, leaving Object (or the bound) and inserting casts. So at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. Kotlin on the JVM erases too, but inline fun <reified T> keeps the type in inline functions.

class Box<T> { private T v; Box(T v){ this.v = v; } T get(){ return v; } }
Box<String> b = new Box<>("hi");
String s = b.get();                    // compiler inserts (String) cast

static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }
class Box<T>(val v: T)
fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T) = if (a >= b) a else b
inline fun <reified T> isA(x: Any) = x is T      // possible only because inlined

Consequences of erasure. No new T(), no T[] creation, no instanceof List<String>, no overloading f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) (same erasure), primitives cannot be type arguments (boxing: List<Integer>, a 16-byte object versus a 4-byte int).

Worked example. List<Integer> of 1M numbers: about 16 MB for objects plus 4 MB references = 20 MB versus 4 MB for int[]. Hence Android's SparseIntArray and Kotlin IntArray.

Industry examples. Gson needs TypeToken<List<Foo>>(){} to recover the type lost by erasure; Retrofit uses the same trick for response types. Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference solves it too.

Everyday analogy. A labelled lunch box: the label is checked at packing time, then thrown away; at lunch you just open it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing generics exist at runtime.
  • Raw types (List without <>) turn off checks; heap pollution.
  • Arrays are reified and covariant; generics are erased and invariant. Mixing them gives warnings.

notes.title: Variance: invariance, covariance, contravariance
notes.html:
Variance answers: if Dog is an Animal, is List<Dog> a List<Animal>? In Java generics, no (invariant), because otherwise you could add a Cat to a list of dogs.

Rules of thumb:

  • Producer (you only read from it): covariant, ? extends T (Java) / out T (Kotlin).
  • Consumer (you only write to it): contravariant, ? super T (Java) / in T (Kotlin).
  • Both: invariant.

Mnemonic: PECS = Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

static double sum(List<? extends Number> src) { double t = 0; for (Number n : src) t += n.doubleValue(); return t; }   // read only
static void fill(List<? super Integer> dst) { dst.add(1); dst.add(2); }                                            // write only
sum(List.of(1, 2.5));              // List<Integer>, List<Double> both OK
fill(new ArrayList<Number>());     // OK
interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }          // can only produce T
interface Sink<in T> { fun put(x: T) }             // can only consume T
fun copy(from: List<out Number>, to: MutableList<in Number>) { to.addAll(from) }
Dog <: Animal
List<Dog>            is NOT a List<Animal>        (invariant)
List<? extends Animal>  accepts List<Dog>         (covariant, read only)
List<? super Dog>       accepts List<Animal>      (contravariant, write only)
Arrays: Dog[] IS an Animal[]  -> ArrayStoreException at runtime if you store a Cat

Worked example. Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the JDK's own PECS signature: reads from src, writes into dest.

Industry examples. Kotlin's read-only List<out E> is covariant, so List<Dog> is a List<Animal>, while MutableList<E> is invariant. Kotlin Function1<in P, out R> explains why a lambda accepting Animal can be used where one accepting Dog is needed. RxJava/Flow Observable<out T>.

Decision gravity. Choosing variance in a public API is a one-way door: narrowing later breaks callers. Use wildcards in parameters, not return types (returning List<? extends X> burdens callers).

Everyday analogy. A fruit basket labelled "apples" cannot be handed to someone who wants "fruit" to add oranges to; but a "fruit basket" can be accepted by anyone who only wants to take out fruit.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up extends and super; use PECS.
  • Trying to add to a List<? extends Number> (only null is allowed).
  • Forgetting that Java arrays are covariant, causing runtime ArrayStoreException.

notes.title: Exception design
notes.html:
Exceptions signal that a method cannot keep its promise. Design them so callers can react correctly and debugging is easy.

Java types: checked (Exception, compiler forces handling; for recoverable conditions the caller can act on, such as IOException) versus unchecked (RuntimeException, programming errors or unrecoverable such as NullPointerException). Kotlin has no checked exceptions.

Rules that work in practice:

  1. Throw early (validate arguments), catch late (where you can recover).
  2. Never swallow: empty catch hides bugs. Log once with context or rethrow.
  3. Wrap with the cause: throw new OrderException("save failed id=" + id, e).
  4. Model failures as part of the API when they are expected (not found, validation): return Optional, Result, or a sealed type instead of throwing for normal flow.
  5. Release resources with try-with-resources / Kotlin use.
try (var conn = ds.getConnection(); var ps = conn.prepareStatement(SQL)) {
    ps.setLong(1, id);
    return map(ps.executeQuery());
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new RepositoryException("load order " + id, e);   // keep cause
}
sealed interface Outcome<out T>
data class Ok<T>(val v: T) : Outcome<T>
data class Fail(val reason: String) : Outcome<Nothing>
fun parse(s: String): Outcome<Int> = s.toIntOrNull()?.let(::Ok) ?: Fail("not a number: $s")

Worked example. A payment call failing. Catch TimeoutException and retry up to 3 times with backoff (200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms); catch CardDeclined and show the user a message (no retry); let NullPointerException crash and alert. Different failures need different reactions, so they need different types.

Cost. Creating an exception fills the stack trace (microseconds, deeper stack costs more); throwing in a hot loop is slow. Disable the trace for control-flow exceptions only if you must.

Industry examples. Spring translates SQLException into unchecked DataAccessException; Kotlin coroutines use CancellationException which you must not swallow; Android crashes on uncaught exceptions on the main thread (ANR/crash rate is a Play Store vital).

Everyday analogy. A smoke alarm with different sounds: fire, low battery, power cut. Each needs a different response.

Common interview traps.

  • catch (Exception e) {} or catch (Throwable).
  • Losing the original cause by throwing a new exception without chaining.
  • Using exceptions for normal control flow.
  • finally that returns, which swallows exceptions.
  • Catching CancellationException in coroutines and breaking cancellation.

notes.title: Interfaces vs abstract classes
notes.html:
An interface defines what something can do (a contract); an abstract class defines what something is, with shared state and partial code.

Interface Abstract class
State (fields) Constants only (Java); Kotlin properties without backing field Yes, instance fields
Inheritance A class can implement many Only one parent
Constructor No Yes
Methods Abstract, plus default/static/private Any mix
Use for Capabilities, plug-in points, API boundaries Shared base with common state and template steps 
interface Flyer { void fly(); }
interface Swimmer { void swim(); }
class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer { public void fly(){} public void swim(){} }

abstract class Report {                       // template method
    final String build() { return header() + body() + footer(); }
    abstract String body();
    String header() { return "REPORT\n"; }
    String footer() { return "\n-- end --"; }
}
interface Flyer { fun fly() }
abstract class Report {
    fun build() = header() + body() + footer()
    abstract fun body(): String
    open fun header() = "REPORT\n"
    open fun footer() = "\n-- end --"
}

Decision rule. Default to an interface. Use an abstract class only when subclasses truly share state or need a fixed algorithm skeleton, and you control all subclasses. Often best: an interface for the contract plus an optional abstract skeleton (JDK: List and AbstractList).

Decision gravity. Interfaces are easy to add for new types; adding an abstract method to a published interface breaks all implementers (before default methods). Choosing an abstract base class locks your users' single inheritance slot: a one-way door.

Industry examples. Android Context (abstract class) versus click-listener interfaces; Java collections; Kotlin delegation class A(b: B) : B by b for reuse without inheritance.

Everyday analogy. An interface is a job description ("can drive"); an abstract class is a half-built house you finish.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying interfaces cannot have code (not since Java 8).
  • Deep abstract hierarchies (fragile base class problem).
  • Forgetting a class can have only one superclass but many interfaces.

notes.title: Default methods and the diamond
notes.html:
A default method is an interface method with a body. Added in Java 8 so libraries could add methods (like List.sort, forEach) without breaking every implementer.

Conflict rule: if two interfaces provide the same default, the class MUST override and may pick one with A.super.m(). A class method always wins over an interface default.

interface Logger { default void log(String m) { System.out.println("[LOG] " + m); } }
interface Auditor { default void log(String m) { System.out.println("[AUDIT] " + m); } }
class Service implements Logger, Auditor {
    @Override public void log(String m) { Logger.super.log(m); Auditor.super.log(m); }   // forced to resolve
}
interface Logger { fun log(m: String) = println("[LOG] $m") }
interface Auditor { fun log(m: String) = println("[AUDIT] $m") }
class Service : Logger, Auditor {
    override fun log(m: String) { super<Logger>.log(m); super<Auditor>.log(m) }
}
Resolution order:
1. Class (or superclass) method wins
2. Else the most specific interface default wins
3. Else compile error -> you must override explicitly

Worked example. JDK 8 added Collection.stream() and Map.getOrDefault() as defaults; millions of existing custom collections kept compiling. Android's minSdk caveat: default methods need desugaring on old API levels (D8 handles it; confirm your AGP version).

Decision gravity. Defaults are for evolving an API safely, not for stuffing logic into interfaces. A default can only use other interface methods (no state), and removing one later is breaking.

Everyday analogy. A standard clause in a contract that applies unless you write your own.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing the diamond resolution rules.
  • Using defaults as a way to simulate multiple inheritance of state.
  • Static interface methods are not inherited by implementers.

notes.title: Sealed types
notes.html:
A sealed type restricts which classes may extend it. The compiler then knows the full list, so a switch/when over it can be checked for completeness without a default.

Java 17 sealed ... permits; Kotlin sealed class/interface (subclasses in the same package and module).

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape {}

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {                     // Java 21 pattern matching; no default needed
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Rect r -> r.w() * r.h();
    };
}
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape
fun area(s: Shape) = when (s) {
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.r * s.r
    is Rect -> s.w * s.h
}

Worked example. UI state in Android: sealed interface UiState { Loading; Success(data); Error(msg) }. Add Empty and the compiler highlights all 6 screens that forgot to render it. That is a free review.

Decision gravity. Sealed = closed set, great for state machines and results (algebraic data types). Open for plugins? Use an interface. Adding a case later is easy inside your own module and forces handling; but external callers can never add cases (by design).

Industry examples. Kotlin Result, coroutines Flow events, Redux/MVI states, Java Optional-like designs, protocol message types.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light has exactly three colours; the rulebook can cover all three, and a fourth would be a rule change everyone must read.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing sealed with final: sealed allows a known few.
  • Using a default/else branch on a sealed switch, which hides new cases.
  • Java requires subclasses to be final, sealed or non-sealed.

notes.title: Records and data classes
notes.html:
A record (Java 16+) or data class (Kotlin) is a transparent carrier of values. The compiler writes the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from the components.

record Point(int x, int y) {
    Point { if (x < 0 || y < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative"); }   // compact constructor
    double dist() { return Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y); }
}
var p = new Point(3, 4);   // p.x(), p.equals(...), toString -> Point[x=3, y=4]
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    init { require(x >= 0 && y >= 0) { "negative" } }
}
val (x, y) = Point(3, 4)           // destructuring
val moved = Point(3, 4).copy(y = 9)
Generated for you:
constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString
Kotlin extra: copy(), componentN() for destructuring
Record: final class, fields private final, cannot extend other classes (can implement interfaces)

Worked example. A hand-written DTO with 5 fields is about 60 lines (fields, constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString). The record is 1 line, and every future field is auto-included in equals, removing a classic "forgot to update equals" bug.

Caveats (senior). Records are shallowly immutable: a List component can still be mutated; copy it in the compact constructor with List.copyOf. Kotlin data class with var is mutable and bad as a map key. Do not use data classes as JPA entities without care (generated equals over all fields, proxies, ids). Adding a field changes equals, the constructor, and serialization shape. A data class's copy is shallow.

Industry examples. DTOs for REST (Jackson supports records), Kotlin Room entities (data classes), UI state, Kafka event payloads, Map.Entry-like pairs.

Everyday analogy. A form with labelled boxes; two forms are the same if every box matches.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing records are deeply immutable.
  • Putting behaviour-heavy domain logic with identity into a record; use a class when identity matters more than values.
  • Forgetting that Kotlin data class needs at least one constructor parameter, and that only primary-constructor properties join equals.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Generics are compile-time checks; erasure removes them at runtime, so no new T(), no instanceof List<String>; Kotlin reified works only in inline functions.
  • Variance: PECS. Producer = ? extends / out, Consumer = ? super / in; generics are invariant by default, arrays covariant.
  • Exceptions: throw early, catch late, chain the cause, never swallow; use Optional/sealed results for expected failures; try-with-resources.
  • Interface for capabilities (default choice), abstract class for shared state or template methods; pair them (interface plus skeleton).
  • Default methods evolve APIs; diamond conflicts must be resolved with X.super.m() and class methods win.
  • Sealed types give closed hierarchies with exhaustive switch/when; records/data classes remove boilerplate but are only shallowly immutable.

questions.promptHtml: What is type erasure, and what can't you do in Java because of it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you know generics are a compile-time feature with real runtime limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The compiler checks generic types, then removes them: List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime, with casts inserted where needed. So you cannot do new T(), new T[n], x instanceof List<String>, or overload on the type argument, and primitives can't be type arguments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
source:    List<String> l; String s = l.get(0);
bytecode:  List l;         String s = (String) l.get(0);

A bounded T extends Comparable<T> erases to Comparable. The reason is backward compatibility with pre-5 code. Kotlin erases on the JVM too, but inline fun <reified T> keeps the type because the body is copied to the call site.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }
// new T();  T[] a = new T[3];  o instanceof List<String>  -> compile errors
inline fun <reified T> isA(x: Any) = x is T

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing generics exist at runtime.
  • Raw types switch off checks.
  • Boxing: List<Integer> of 1M numbers is about 20 MB versus 4 MB for int[].

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Gson read List<Foo>? -> TypeToken captures the generic superclass signature, which is kept in class metadata.
  2. Why can't I overload f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>)? -> Same erasure.
  3. What is heap pollution? -> A variable of a parameterized type that refers to an object of the wrong type, causing a late ClassCastException.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "no generics at runtime". Senior: bridge methods, reified, TypeToken tricks, boxing cost, and why Valhalla matters.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: JSON parsing into List<Foo> returned maps and exploded far from the parse site.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, and which would you throw from your own API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes API design judgement, not just syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Checked exceptions are forced by the compiler for conditions the caller can reasonably recover from; unchecked ones signal programming errors or unrecoverable states. In my APIs I use unchecked by default, checked when callers must make a recovery decision, and return types (Optional or a sealed result) for expected outcomes like "not found".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Rules that survive production: throw early, catch late; chain causes; never swallow; use try-with-resources. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, and Spring converts SQLException into unchecked DataAccessException. Cost: building an exception fills the stack trace, a few microseconds, more for deep stacks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
try (var conn = ds.getConnection(); var ps = conn.prepareStatement(SQL)) {
    ps.setLong(1, id);
    return map(ps.executeQuery());
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new RepositoryException("load order " + id, e);   // keeps the cause
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (Exception e) {}.
  • Throwing a new exception without the cause.
  • Using exceptions for normal control flow.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is Optional better than throwing? -> When absence is a normal result.
  2. What does finally { return x; } do? -> It swallows any in-flight exception.
  3. How do you handle exceptions across layers? -> Translate at the boundary and keep the cause.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average repeats the textbook split. Senior discusses translation at layer boundaries, failure as part of the type, and observability (log once).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Swallowed exceptions hid a failing payment webhook for days.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use an interface and when an abstract class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A staple that reveals design maturity beyond "interfaces have no code".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Interface for a capability or contract; abstract class when subclasses share state or a fixed algorithm skeleton and I control all subclasses. Default to the interface because a class can implement many but extend only one. Often I offer both: an interface plus an optional abstract skeleton.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Interface Abstract class
State none (constants) fields
Constructors no yes
Inheritance many one
Methods abstract, default, static any

Template method fits an abstract class; plug-in points fit an interface. JDK example: List with AbstractList.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Flyer { fun fly() }
abstract class Report {
    fun build() = header() + body() + footer()
    abstract fun body(): String
    open fun header() = "REPORT\n"
    open fun footer() = "\n-- end --"
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Interfaces cannot have code" (false since Java 8).
  • Deep abstract hierarchies.
  • Using an abstract class just to share two helper methods.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an interface hold state? -> Only constants; Kotlin properties without backing fields.
  2. Why prefer interfaces for public APIs? -> Do not consume the user's single inheritance slot.
  3. How do you evolve an interface? -> default methods.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average gives the feature table. Senior frames it as evolution cost and one-way doors.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Extending a framework base class blocked a team from also extending another.

questions.contextHtml:
A report job fails at 02:10 nightly with a ClassCastException deep inside a formatter, 4 stack frames away from where bad data entered.

List<String> names = loadNames();            // returns List<String>
addIds(names);                               // legacy helper
for (String n : names) out.print(n.trim());  // boom

static void addIds(List list) { list.add(42); }   // raw type
java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String
    at Report.format(Report.java:57)

Red herrings: "bad DB data", "a recent JDK upgrade".
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you prevent this class of bug?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Validate the data." The problem is a type hole, not the data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Any -Xlint warnings? Who calls addIds? Is the project mixing old and new code?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the helper signature.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) raw List parameter allows heap pollution; (b) unchecked cast elsewhere; (c) deserialization bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: compile with -Xlint:unchecked,rawtypes; grep for raw types; set a breakpoint on list.add in the helper.
  5. Root cause: Erasure means the runtime does not know the list holds strings; the raw call compiles with a warning and the cast is inserted only where the value is read.
  6. Fix: static void addIds(List<? super Integer> list) and a separate List<Integer>; never reuse the list.
  7. Prevention: -Werror on unchecked/rawtypes, Error Prone RawTypes, review rule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") only with a comment proving safety.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Collections.checkedList? -> Fails at insertion time, useful in tests.
  • Kotlin? -> Star-projections and as unchecked casts have the same hole.
  • Why does the stack trace point elsewhere? -> The cast is at the read site.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An old XML library returned raw lists; a single -Werror flag exposed 60 hidden type holes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames data.
  • Hire: spots raw type and erasure.
  • Strong hire: adds lint, checkedList and a safe signature.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Variance questions reveal whether a candidate really understands generics rather than copying signatures.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If I could pass a List<Dog> as List<Animal>, someone could add a Cat to it. So generics are invariant. If I only read from it (producer) I use ? extends T; if I only write to it (consumer) I use ? super T. Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
List<? extends Animal>  accepts List<Dog>   -> read Animal, cannot add (except null)
List<? super Dog>       accepts List<Animal> -> add Dog, read only Object
Dog[] IS an Animal[]    -> ArrayStoreException at runtime

Kotlin states variance at the declaration: Source<out T> (producer), Sink<in T> (consumer). Read-only List<out E> is covariant, MutableList<E> invariant. Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the canonical example.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static double sum(List<? extends Number> src) { double t = 0; for (Number n : src) t += n.doubleValue(); return t; }
static void fill(List<? super Integer> dst) { dst.add(1); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Swapping extends/super.
  • Using wildcards in return types.
  • Forgetting arrays are covariant.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't you add to List<? extends Number>? -> The actual element type is unknown.
  2. Kotlin in/out vs wildcards? -> Declaration-site versus use-site variance.
  3. Why Function<in P, out R>? -> A function accepting Animal can stand in for one needing Dog.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average recites PECS. Senior derives it from the cat/dog proof and treats variance as an API one-way door.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A utility with List<Number> parameters could not take List<Integer>, forcing copies everywhere.

questions.contextHtml:
An order service is returning HTTP 200 with an empty body for about 0.8% of requests during a database failover. Logs show nothing at ERROR. The code:

Order load(long id) {
    try {
        return repo.find(id);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        // TODO handle
    }
    return null;
}
String parse(String s) {
    try { return Json.parse(s); }
    finally { return "{}"; }
}

Metrics: db_connection_errors_total rose by 4,100 during the same 6 minutes; 5xx rate flat.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add logging in the catch." Better, but the API still reports success on failure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do callers do with null? Is there a retry layer? Which exceptions can find throw?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make failures visible: rethrow so the platform returns 503 and retries work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) swallowed SQLException; (b) finally return swallows parse errors; (c) null treated as "not found".
  4. How I'd verify each: compare db error counter and empty-body count by timestamp; grep for empty catches; unit test with a failing repo.
  5. Root cause: Exceptions were converted to null, losing meaning; callers cannot tell "missing" from "broken".
  6. Fix: distinguish expected from unexpected.
Optional<Order> find(long id) {                       // absence is normal
    try { return repo.find(id); }
    catch (SQLException e) { throw new RepositoryException("load order " + id, e); }
}

Remove return in finally. 7. Prevention: Error Prone EmptyCatch, FinallyJump; alert when errors with no log; contract tests with a failing fake. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not log and rethrow at every layer (duplicate noise); log once at the boundary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retry on failure? -> Only for idempotent reads, with backoff and a cap.
  • Should null ever be returned? -> Not as an error signal.
  • Why is a finally return dangerous? -> It discards any exception, even Error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payment confirmation path swallowed timeouts; reconciliation found 312 orders charged but unfulfilled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds a log line.
  • Hire: stops swallowing, separates not-found from failure.
  • Strong hire: adds translation, lint, and log-once policy.

questions.contextHtml:
Your platform library ships interface Audit { default void log(String m) {...} }. Another team's module has class Service implements Logger, Audit where Logger already had default void log(String). The upgrade to library 2.0 breaks their build; 14 services fail to compile on Friday before a release.

error: types Logger and Audit are incompatible;
  class Service inherits unrelated defaults for log(String) from types Logger and Audit

Red herring: "pin the old library forever".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and how to roll this out safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Interfaces can't have code" or "remove the default."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the method name necessary? Binary vs source compatibility requirements? How many implementers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin consumers to 1.x or ship 2.0.1 renaming the default.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two unrelated defaults with the same signature; (b) a class method wins only if it exists; (c) abstract redeclaration.
  4. How I'd verify each: compile a minimal repro; javap the class for bridge/default info.
  5. Root cause: The diamond rule: no class method, no more specific interface, so the compiler demands an explicit override.
  6. Fix: consumers override and choose.
class Service implements Logger, Audit {
    @Override public void log(String m) { Logger.super.log(m); Audit.super.log(m); }
}

Library-side: rename to audit(String). 7. Prevention: Treat adding a default method as a potentially source-breaking change; japicmp/revapi checks; deprecation cycle. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not stuff logic into interface defaults to emulate multiple inheritance.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Binary compatibility? -> Already-compiled classes would throw IncompatibleClassChangeError at runtime.
  • Class method vs interface default? -> Class wins.
  • Kotlin? -> Must override and use super<Logger>.log(m).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework added default close() to a base interface and silently overlapped with a user's AutoCloseable default across 30 modules.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: unaware of defaults conflict.
  • Hire: explains rule and X.super.m().
  • Strong hire: raises binary compatibility and API-diff tooling.

questions.contextHtml:
An Android app models screen state. A new Empty state is added for a zero-result search. QA reports that the search screen shows an endless spinner for empty results, 3 of 6 screens affected. No compile error.

sealed interface UiState {
    object Loading : UiState
    data class Success(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState
    object Empty : UiState            // NEW
}
fun render(s: UiState) = when (s) {
    is UiState.Success -> showList(s.items)
    is UiState.Error -> showError(s.msg)
    else -> showSpinner()             // written when only Loading remained
}

Red herring: "the backend returns 200 with an empty body".
questions.promptHtml: Why did the compiler not help, and how do you prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an is Empty branch." Fixes one screen but not the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many when over UiState? Any in Java files or other modules? Is it used as a statement or an expression?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Handle Empty in all 3 offending screens and ship.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) else hides new subclasses; (b) when used as a statement (older Kotlin did not enforce exhaustiveness for statements; newer versions do for sealed, verify your version); (c) state not emitted.
  4. How I'd verify each: grep is UiState and else ->; remove else and let the compiler list failures.
  5. Root cause: The else branch opts out of exhaustiveness checking.
  6. Fix: remove else everywhere, make when an expression.
fun render(s: UiState) = when (s) {
    UiState.Loading -> showSpinner()
    is UiState.Success -> showList(s.items)
    is UiState.Error -> showError(s.msg)
    UiState.Empty -> showEmpty()
}
  1. Prevention: Lint rule forbidding else on sealed when; screenshot tests per state.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not make a state a plain enum with a catch-all; sealed gives payloads plus checking. External modules can't add cases by design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Java 21 equivalent? -> switch over a sealed interface without default.
  • What if plugins must add states? -> Use an open interface, not sealed.
  • Serialization of sealed hierarchies? -> Needs a polymorphic registry (verify per library).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Adding a Offline state exposed 11 forgotten renderers at compile time once a team deleted all else branches.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches one screen.
  • Hire: removes else and uses exhaustive when.
  • Strong hire: adds lint and discusses sealed vs open trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: What do records and data classes give you, and what are their limits? Are they immutable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know "shallow immutability" and the pitfalls beyond less boilerplate.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: They generate the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from the components, so value semantics are free and consistent. They are only shallowly immutable: a List component can still change. Kotlin adds copy and destructuring; a Kotlin data class with var is mutable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Record: final class, private final fields, can implement interfaces, cannot extend a class; compact constructor validates.
  • Data class: only primary-constructor properties join equals; copy() is shallow.
  • Adding a field changes equals, the constructor and serialization shape.
  • Avoid for JPA entities (identity, proxies, lazy collections).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
record Order(String id, List<String> items) {
    Order { items = List.copyOf(items); if (id.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }
}
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)
val moved = Point(3, 4).copy(y = 9)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking records are deeply immutable.
  • Using a record where identity matters more than value.
  • Expecting body properties of a data class in equals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a record have a mutable field? -> Not an instance field beyond components; a component can be a mutable object.
  2. Binary compatibility when adding a component? -> Breaks constructors and deserialization.
  3. Data class as a map key? -> Safe only with val and immutable components.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "less boilerplate". Senior: shallow immutability, evolution cost, entity misuse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A record DTO holding a mutable List was altered by a consumer, corrupting a cached response.

questions.contextHtml:
You are designing a public EventBus library used by 40 internal teams. Draft signatures:

void publish(List<Event> events);
List<? extends Event> drain();
void subscribe(Handler<Event> h);
interface Handler<T> { void on(T e); }

Early users complain: they cannot pass a List<OrderEvent> to publish, cannot register a Handler<Object> for logging, and callers of drain() cannot add to the result. A teammate also proposes returning Event[] for speed.
questions.promptHtml: Fix the signatures with variance and justify each choice, including the array proposal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Makes everything ? extends or ?; or accepts arrays because "they're faster".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do handlers mutate events? Is the list retained after publish? Frequency (1M events/s)? Binary compatibility promises?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a patch release widening parameters (source compatible).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) invariant parameters reject legitimate callers; (b) wildcards in returns burden callers; (c) arrays covariant, unsafe.
  4. How I'd verify each: compile samples from three teams against the draft; try Handler<Object>.
  5. Root cause: Producer parameters should be ? extends, consumers ? super, and return types concrete.
  6. Fix:
void publish(Collection<? extends Event> events);   // we only read
<T extends Event> void subscribe(Class<T> type, Handler<? super T> h);  // handler consumes T
List<Event> drain();                                  // concrete return (copy)

Not arrays: covariant arrays give ArrayStoreException at runtime; copy cost is small. 7. Prevention: Example-based API tests; japicmp. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not return wildcards; do not overuse wildcards where a plain type parameter reads better. Variance in a public API is a one-way door; widening later is compatible, narrowing is not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Kotlin version? -> fun publish(events: Collection<Event>) works because read-only collections are out; handler Handler<in T>.
  • Why pass Class<T>? -> Erasure; needed to route at runtime.
  • Mutability of the list inside publish? -> Copy defensively if retained.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A metrics SDK signature List<Metric> forced 200 call sites to copy lists; widening it to Collection<? extends Metric> fixed them with no downstream change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random wildcards.
  • Hire: correct PECS on parameters.
  • Strong hire: justifies concrete returns, rejects arrays, discusses compatibility.

questions.contextHtml:
An Android app's profile screen leaks. Leak canary shows ProfileViewModel retained after the user left the screen; ANR rate rose from 0.2% to 0.9% after a release. A diff shows a "make it robust" change:

viewModelScope.launch {
    try {
        val p = api.loadProfile()      // suspend, can be cancelled
        render(p)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        log.warn("load failed", e)
        retryLoop()                    // keeps running
    }
}
W/Profile: load failed  kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled

Red herrings: "network is flaky", "increase timeout".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a longer timeout." Cancellation is intended, not an error.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does retryLoop do? Is the scope tied to the lifecycle? Do other launches catch broadly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rethrow CancellationException.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) catch (Exception) swallows CancellationException, so the coroutine continues after cancellation; (b) scope not cancelled; (c) blocking call in the retry.
  4. How I'd verify each: log isActive in retryLoop; heap dump for ProfileViewModel; Android Studio coroutine debugger.
  5. Root cause: Cancellation is delivered as an exception; swallowing it breaks structured concurrency.
  6. Fix:
try { render(api.loadProfile()) }
catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
catch (e: IOException) { log.warn("load failed", e); retryWithBackoff() }

Prefer catching specific exceptions; call ensureActive() in loops. 7. Prevention: Detekt TooGenericExceptionCaught, SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation; tests with runTest that cancel. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No catch (Throwable). Use runCatching carefully: it also catches cancellation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cleanup on cancel? -> finally with withContext(NonCancellable).
  • Does withTimeout throw it? -> TimeoutCancellationException, a subclass; handle it differently.
  • Same problem in Java? -> InterruptedException must be restored with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A blanket catch (Exception) in a sync worker made it ignore shutdown, delaying deploys by 90 seconds every time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes timeouts.
  • Hire: identifies swallowed cancellation and rethrows.
  • Strong hire: specific catch policy, NonCancellable cleanup, lint.

questions.promptHtml: You own a widely used library type. How do interface versus abstract class affect your ability to evolve it over five years?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Looks for one-way-door thinking and knowledge of compatibility, not just feature lists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An interface lets me add default methods without breaking implementers, but removing or changing is breaking; an abstract class uses up the user's only superclass slot and exposes protected hooks that become frozen contracts. I publish an interface and an optional abstract skeleton, keep the class hierarchy shallow, and use final or sealed where I don't want extension.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Adding an abstract method: source and binary breaking for both.
  • Adding a default method: source-compatible mostly, but can create diamond conflicts (see conflicts rule: class wins, else compile error).
  • Fragile base class: subclasses depend on calls the base makes internally (the CountingSet problem).
  • Binary compatibility: callers compiled against old versions break with AbstractMethodError/IncompatibleClassChangeError.
  • Sealed or final: explicit statement of "do not extend".
Interface + AbstractSkeleton   (JDK: List + AbstractList)
  users choose: implement fully, or extend skeleton

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Store { fun get(k: String): String?; fun getOrDefault(k: String, d: String) = get(k) ?: d }
abstract class SkeletalStore : Store { /* shared caching */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using default methods as a dumping ground.
  • Leaving classes open "just in case".
  • Not running API diff tools.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Static methods on interfaces? -> Not inherited, good for factories.
  2. How do you deprecate? -> @Deprecated with forRemoval and a release cycle.
  3. How do tools check? -> japicmp, revapi, Kotlin binary-compatibility-validator.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: table of differences. Senior: compatibility matrices and the cost of each choice years later.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A framework added an abstract method to a base class and broke dozens of downstream modules at runtime.

questions.contextHtml:
After a refactor, a pricing service reads rules from JSON into a generic helper. It works in unit tests but fails in production 2 minutes after startup.

static <T> List<T> readList(String json, Class<T> type) {
    return gson.fromJson(json, List.class);           // refactored from a typed call
}
List<Rule> rules = readList(json, Rule.class);
double d = rules.get(0).discount;                      // fails later
java.lang.ClassCastException: class com.google.gson.internal.LinkedTreeMap
  cannot be cast to class Rule
    at Pricing.apply(Pricing.java:88)

Red herrings: "Gson version", "JSON field names changed".
questions.promptHtml: Why does this compile and break late? How do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a Rule constructor". Not about the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which library? Does a cache hold the pre-built list? Why did tests pass (they used empty lists or Mockito)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert to the typed call.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) List.class loses the element type, giving List<LinkedTreeMap>; (b) unchecked generic return; (c) wrong types in JSON.
  4. How I'd verify each: print rules.get(0).getClass(); inspect the warning list.
  5. Root cause: Erasure: the library cannot see T; the unchecked cast hides it until an element is used as Rule.
  6. Fix: capture the generic type.
Type t = TypeToken.getParameterized(List.class, type).getType();
List<T> out = gson.fromJson(json, t);

Kotlin alternative: inline fun <reified T> Gson.readList(json: String). 7. Prevention: Tests with non-empty fixtures; compile with unchecked warnings as errors. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No blanket @SuppressWarnings; do not cast manually element by element.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retrofit equivalent? -> Response types come from Type in the method signature.
  • Jackson? -> TypeReference.
  • Why not store Class<List<Rule>>? -> It does not exist.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared cache helper returned maps instead of DTOs for a week; the failure appeared only in the branch that read a field.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random edits.
  • Hire: identifies erasure and uses TypeToken.
  • Strong hire: reified alternative, test strategy and lint.

questions.contextHtml:
A validation endpoint at 50,000 requests/second spends 22% of CPU in Throwable.fillInStackTrace. 35% of requests contain invalid input and the code throws ValidationException for each, from 9 frames deep within a framework stack of about 60 frames.

async-profiler: 22.4%  java.lang.Throwable.fillInStackTrace
                 6.1%  ValidationException.<init>
p99 latency 180 ms (SLO 100 ms)

Red herring: "GC pauses".
questions.promptHtml: Redesign error handling to hit the SLO without hiding real failures.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable stack traces everywhere" (kills debugging for real errors).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are invalid inputs expected user mistakes? Which layers need the exception? Do callers branch on it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Override fillInStackTrace (or use the 4-arg constructor with writableStackTrace=false) for this expected exception only.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stack capture cost for expected failures; (b) log serialization of traces; (c) deep proxy stacks.
  4. How I'd verify each: async-profiler flame graph, count of exceptions/s, JMH of throwing 9 frames deep.
  5. Root cause: Using exceptions for a normal outcome (35%) pays the stack walk each time.
  6. Fix: return a result type from the validator.
sealed interface Validation { object Ok : Validation; data class Invalid(val errors: List<String>) : Validation }
fun validate(r: Request): Validation = if (r.name.isBlank()) Invalid(listOf("name")) else Ok

Keep exceptions for genuinely exceptional cases (DB down). 7. Prevention: Metric "exceptions per second" per type; code review rule: expected failures are values. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not suppress traces globally; do not use sealed results where 15 layers must propagate them (use exceptions there).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Preallocated singleton exception? -> Works, but has no useful context and shares state; avoid.
  • Spring @ExceptionHandler still needed? -> For unexpected failures, yes.
  • Kotlin Result? -> Fine inside a module; avoid in public API or coroutines pitfalls (verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replacing validation exceptions with a result type cut CPU by a fifth on a signup flow and made error messages testable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables traces blindly.
  • Hire: results for expected failures.
  • Strong hire: measured with profiler, scoped trace suppression, clear policy.
